Hamiltonian in an Atomic Orbital Basis

Bloch States

In a localized atomic orbital basis, a Bloch state can be expanded as [1]

\[|\nu\mathbf{k}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{n}} \sum_{j\beta} C^{\mathbf{k},\nu}_{j\beta}|\phi_{nj\beta}\rangle,\]

where \(\nu\) is the band index, \(\mathbf{k}\) is the crystal wave vector, and \(N\) is the number of unit cells in the Born-von Kármán supercell. The lattice vector \(\mathbf{R}_{n}\) locates the \(n\)-th unit cell, \(j\) labels an atom within that cell, and \(\beta\) labels an orbital on that atom. The coefficients \(C^{\mathbf{k},\nu}_{j\beta}\) specify the expansion of the Bloch state. The localized orbitals are defined by

\[\langle\mathbf{r}|\phi_{nj\beta}\rangle = \phi_{j\beta}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_{n}-\boldsymbol{\tau}_{j}),\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{j}\) is the position of atom \(j\) relative to the origin of its unit cell. Here, the Bloch phase contains only the lattice vector \(\mathbf{R}_{n}\); the atomic position \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{j}\) is included in the orbital definition. The reciprocal-space matrices below use this same phase convention.

Hamiltonian and Overlap Matrices

Atomic orbitals are generally nonorthogonal. The real-space Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements are defined as

\[\begin{split}H_{mi\alpha,nj\beta} &= \langle\phi_{mi\alpha}|\hat{\mathcal{H}}|\phi_{nj\beta}\rangle, \\ S_{mi\alpha,nj\beta} &= \langle\phi_{mi\alpha}|\phi_{nj\beta}\rangle.\end{split}\]

Assuming that the basis is linearly independent, the overlap matrix \(S\) is invertible. Within the space spanned by this basis, the Hamiltonian operator can be written as

\[\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{AO}} = \sum_{mi\alpha,nj\beta} |\phi_{mi\alpha}\rangle \widetilde{H}_{mi\alpha,nj\beta} \langle\phi_{nj\beta}|, \qquad \widetilde{H}=S^{-1}HS^{-1}.\]

The matrix \(\widetilde{H}\) gives the coefficients of the operator in this outer-product expansion; it differs from the matrix of Hamiltonian elements \(H\). The two factors of \(S^{-1}\) account for the nonorthogonality of the basis. For an orthonormal basis, \(S=I\) and \(\widetilde{H}=H\).

Generalized Eigenvalue Problem

For a periodic system, translational symmetry allows the real-space matrices to be Fourier transformed into reciprocal space:

\[\begin{split}H^{\mathbf{k}}_{i\alpha,j\beta} &= \sum_n \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{n}} H_{0i\alpha,nj\beta}, \\ S^{\mathbf{k}}_{i\alpha,j\beta} &= \sum_n \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{n}} S_{0i\alpha,nj\beta},\end{split}\]

where the index \(0\) denotes the reference cell at \(\mathbf{R}_0=\mathbf{0}\), and the sum runs over relative lattice vectors with Born–von Kármán periodic boundary conditions.

The electronic energies and expansion coefficients are obtained by solving the generalized eigenvalue problem [2]

\[H^{\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{C}_{\nu\mathbf{k}} = \varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}} S^{\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{C}_{\nu\mathbf{k}},\]

where \(\varepsilon_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\) is the energy of the Bloch state \(|\nu\mathbf{k}\rangle\) and the components of \(\mathbf{C}_{\nu\mathbf{k}}\) are \(C^{\mathbf{k},\nu}_{j\beta}\). The eigenvectors are chosen to satisfy the overlap-weighted orthonormality condition

\[\mathbf{C}_{\nu\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger} S^{\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{C}_{\mu\mathbf{k}} = \delta_{\nu\mu},\]

which ensures that the corresponding Bloch states are normalized and mutually orthogonal at each \(\mathbf{k}\).
